title: North Shields mother told to make appointment to give birth to dead baby
description: Image source, Danielle BrownImage caption, Anthony and Danielle now have tattoos of Maisie's hand and footprintByNorth East and Cumbria health corresp
body: Image source, Danielle BrownImage caption, Anthony and Danielle now have tattoos of Maisie's hand and footprintByNorth East and Cumbria health correspondentUpdated 21 minutes agoWarning: This article contains themes and images some readers may find upsetting.A seven-month pregnant woman whose unborn baby died after she was discharged from hospital while suffering from a life-threatening condition was told by staff to make an appointment to give birth.Danielle Brown, 31, from North Tyneside, said she was devastated to have to return home knowing the baby she was carrying was no longer alive.She said no family should be put through the same experience and wants hospitals to offer alternatives for those grieving.After she was discharged from hospital suffering with pre-eclampsia, Danielle insisted on returning to the maternity unit as she felt so unwell and was seen by doctors.She was told her her daughter had died, but, instead of delivering the baby, the hospital sent her home and told to book a slot to give birth.Her partner Anthony Miller, 34, described it as "horrible... lying in bed and holding that belly" knowing their baby was not alive.The Newcastle Hospitals NHS Trust said it fully accepted "aspects of the care we provided fell short" and offered a "heartfelt apology".Image source, Danielle BrownImage caption, Anthony and Danielle were overjoyed to learn they were having a girlDanielle and Anthony had been delighted to learn they were having a baby girl, who they decided to call Maisie."I was just over the moon, I couldn't be happier," Anthony said. But in February 2023, seven months into her pregnancy, Danielle woke up feeling unwell. Her face was swollen, as were her hands and feet - all potential signs of pre-eclampsia, external, which can be life threatening to both mother and baby.The couple went to the Northumbria Specialist Emergency Care Hospital in Cramlington, Northumberland, but medics found problems with Maisie's heart rate and told Danielle her baby needed to be delivered immediately via emergency caesarean section, external. "Maisie's heart rate had dropped and a midwife ran in and said 'don't panic, but I need to pull the emergency cord - you're having your baby'," Danielle said.The midwife told her space was being found for her at the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI) in Newcastle and doctors there "were going to do the section", she said. She was transferred by ambulance but, once in Newcastle, Danielle did not have the operation and was instead put on a ward. "A consultant came to see me and he said I am staying in hospital until Maisie was born," she said.But, the following day, another doctor reviewed her and sent her home. Image source, Danielle BrownImage caption, A normal scan showed Maisie at 16 weeks Within 24 hours, again feeling unwell, Danielle called the maternity unit and said she was told she probably had a stomach bug. But she insisted on being seen."When I finally had a scan, the screen was turned away and there was no sound," Danielle said. She remembers turning to her partner and saying: "I think she's gone."Doctors were unable to find Maisie's heartbeat and they told Danielle her baby had died.But instead of delivering the baby, as she expected, Danielle was given a phone number, and sent home. She said they told her to "give us a call on Friday morning, and book a slot to come in and have Maisie". At home the couple struggled to cope. "It was horrible," Anthony said. "Lying in bed and holding that belly, and still being able to feel Maisie but knowing she wasn't alive." Two days later, after 10 hours in labour, Danielle gave birth."When Maisie was born the room was silent," she said. "Seeing Maisie was bittersweet. She was perfect. I told her she was beautiful and I loved her. "It was devastating that my first experience of holding a baby was holding my stillborn daughter."Image source, Danielle BrownImage caption, Danielle and Anthony finally held Maisie two days after being told of her deathSpeaking publicly for the first time about what happened, Danielle said no-one should be sent home still carrying a baby who has died. "Don't," she said. "Just take that family and help them. Help them.  "When we left hospital, we gave Maisie one last cuddle and kiss and told her we loved her and were sorry things couldn't have been different."After saying goodbye to their daughter, the couple faced further distress. To leave the hospital they had to walk past other parents holding their babies. "We should have been leaving with our baby too, but we were leaving with a memory box," Danielle said. "All the new mums were walking out carrying their babies. That will stay with me forever."The couple want every hospital in the UK to provide an alternative way out for grieving mothers, to "make a different route for a parent who has just lost a child".Image source, Danielle BrownImage caption, Danielle Brown and Anthony Miller had been looking forward to the birth of their baby girl  The trust's executive director of nursing and midwifery, Ian Joy, said: "We fully accept that aspects of the care we provided fell short of the standards the family had every right to expect and offer a heartfelt apology for this."Following a detailed review in 2023, we improved urgent assessment for women who come to our maternity services with unexpected symptoms or suspected complications and introduced quicker escalation procedures when there are concerns."Legal executive Faisal Ali, from the law firm Irwin Mitchell, said pre‑eclampsia could be life‑threatening without appropriate care."What happened to Danielle and Maisie vividly highlights the human cost of care failings," he said."The trust admitted Danielle should not have been discharged on either the 14th or 15th of February 2023. Had she remained in hospital, monitoring would have shown the need to speed up delivery and Maisie would have been born alive."An NHS England spokesperson said: "These failings in care are unacceptable and should never have happened."Anyone experiencing the loss of a baby should be fully supported by a specialist maternity team so they can make choices about their care that are right for them."Follow BBC Newcastle on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.

schema.headline: North Shields mother told to make appointment to give birth to dead baby

title: Shabana Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants
description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will announce her final decision on changes to immigration rules on Monday.Mahmood proposed extending the wait for perm
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will announce her final decision on changes to immigration rules on Monday.Mahmood proposed extending the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10, with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait, in response to a period of high net migration.But she faced criticism for proposing to apply the changes to migrant workers already in the UK, with Housing Secretary Angela Rayner saying this would "change the goalposts".The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently working in social care. The Conservatives said Mahmood had "capitulated control of immigration policy" to Rayner.Many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.The home secretary is expected to announce her final decision in a statement to MPs in the House of Commons.Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.Mahmood announced plans to delay settlements in response to concerns over the number of people approaching eligibility, in the wake of record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Conservative government.The Home Office has said its figures show net migration - the difference between those entering and leaving the country - added 2.6m people to the UK population between 2021 and 2024.The department forecast around 1.6m people could therefore settle between 2026 and 2030.More than 200,000 responses were submitted to the consultation on Mahmood's proposals, which were launched under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.Several Labour MPs raised concerns about the impact of the proposals on migrants already living here, describing the retrospective approach as "un-British". They also warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that settlement is a "right to be earned, not just granted automatically".Mahmood has argued reforms are required to avoid a "drain on our public finances".In her foreword to the consultation, Mahmood said the bar to entry to the UK was "lowered significantly" and this was "most evident in the health and care visa".She wrote: "An attempt to fill between 6,000 and 40,000 jobs saw the arrival of 616,000 individuals from 2022 to 2024."Over half were not even arriving to work in that sector but were instead dependants of those who were."Home Office calculations suggested 196,000 care workers and their adult dependants could settle between 2026 and 2030, at an estimated lifetime cost of £9.5bn to taxpayers.On Monday, the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank said that skilled workers and their dependants due to settle in the UK under current rules are expected to make a net lifetime contribution of around £115bn through the taxes they pay.Former Home Office Minister Mike Tapp told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I very much hope that those who are genuinely working in health and social care for five years are exempt from that retrospective extension to the time they need to be here before they apply for settlement."We've all known someone in our family or friends who has been cared for by these people, so that would be the right thing to do."In June, Mahmood had asked Sir Keir to sack Tapp after he wrote an unauthorised article arguing that foreign care workers should be exempt from the changes to ILR.Dr Ben Brindle, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, said that "at the broader level [the policy] probably won't have too much impact" on people's decision to come to the UK."Immigration policy acts as more of a barrier than anything," he told Today.Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "By Mahmood's own admission in a speech this March, letting low wage care workers alone stay forever will cost taxpayers £10bn and be an 'affront'. "Now she looks likes she's about to do exactly that."Meanwhile, Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said Mahmood had been "overruled" by Burnham, which was "a disaster for Britain". He added that Reform would abolish ILR altogether.

schema.headline: Shabana Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants

title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting al-Shabab
description: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.The first contingent of 109 Ugand
body: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.The first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.Uganda's acting army spokesperson, Chris Magezi, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), which was established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.Last week, Gen Muhoozi said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces."As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.The withdrawal is being carried out in phases and is expected to be completed in August 2027.However, Uganda is not ending its entire military involvement in Somalia. Its troops deployed under a separate bilateral security arrangement will remain in the country.An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside  about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements. Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency led al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, for more than two decades.Uganda forces first deployed to the country in 2007 and played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns. They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.Ugandan troops continued its military involvement under successive Africa Union, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.It was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support. A 12-month transition plan is due to begin to in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

schema.headline: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting al-Shabab

title: Nine killed in fiery Florida Learjet crash in West Palm Beach County
description: Nine killed as small jet crashes on Florida streetFigure caption, Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByCraig HoyleUpdated 2 hours agoA
body: Nine killed as small jet crashes on Florida streetFigure caption, Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByCraig HoyleUpdated 2 hours agoA business jet crashed in a neighbourhood in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people on board, the US transport secretary has said.The crash happened near Cresthaven, some nine miles (14 km) from Mar-a-Lago, President Donald Trump's resort in the wealthy enclave of Palm Beach County, around 12:50 EST (17:50 GMT).Images show a large crater in the middle of a multi-lane road, with fire and debris from the Learjet 60 aircraft scattered across it, but nobody on the ground was hurt.The aircraft had departed from Austin, Texas, and was headed to the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement.Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.In air traffic control audio recorded moments before the crash, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".The person can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.The crew member declared an emergency, yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit was "we're out of time".Image source, ReutersImage caption, A flaming crater at the scene of the crash in FloridaUnverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera  recording of the moment of the crash. It shows vehicles driving on a residential suburban street, when suddenly an aircraft nosedives into the ground almost vertically, and explodes into a large fireball."When you see that video, it's a jarring thing," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters at a news conference after the crash. "It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."It is not yet clear who was aboard the jet when it crashed. DeSantis said "as of now, we don't have any reports of anyone who was on the ground...who was killed or injured".Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash as a "horrific tragedy", and said the FAA was sending a team to the scene to help an investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board."Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost," Duffy added.Palm Beach County Fire Rescue has declared a "mass casualty incident".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The jet crashed on a six-lane roadThe Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants. At a news conference, DeSantis and local officials said that 600 local residents were being evacuated from a nearby trailer-park community.The impact of the crash caused considerable damage to local infrastructure, including its water lines, they said, and it would be at least 30 days before the road re-opened.Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash, and it was heavily raining as the news conference was held.Trump had been at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

schema.headline: Nine killed in fiery Florida Learjet crash in West Palm Beach County

title: Lindsay Clancy will reappear in court - but will her case be retried?
description: Fundamentally, Clancy's legal team - with Reddington at the helm - is pushing for the charges to be dismissed or dropped. They've explored a variety o
body: Fundamentally, Clancy's legal team - with Reddington at the helm - is pushing for the charges to be dismissed or dropped. They've explored a variety of legal avenues. In September, he asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts provision that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not present enough evidence at trial.That request was denied. Judge Sullivan will hear arguments on several motions on Monday, but Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and mental health law expert, told the BBC that the hearing will likely focus on a narrow point: was this an instance of a routine deadlocked-jury mistrial - in which the jury genuinely could not agree - or was this an improperly terminated trial? She said Reddington may argue that a retrial could violate Clancy's Constitutional protection against double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice. But legal experts agree that outcome is unlikely. "The public attention that's been put on this trial and the need to have some conclusion in the near future, I think that the judge is going to say that this mistrial was appropriate, was legally accurate, and that they need to now look to set a date for a retrial," Cucolo said.Judge Sullivan could make a determination over whether the case can proceed on Monday or he could rule later in writing, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC. And how the District Attorney's office wants to proceed could be determined ahead of Monday's hearing, during it or even days after, she said. "The three charges of first-degree murder are still pending; they are still hanging over Lindsay Clancy's head unless and until the DA announces otherwise," Hershon said.Historically, Cruz, the district attorney, has made comments and announcements about the case at press conferences after court finishes. That could happen again this week, she predicted. It is also likely, Hershon said, that Judge Sullivan pushes the lawyers on both sides to get a trial date on the calendar during Monday's hearing. "It does not mean it's definitely going to be a jury trial, but [they will want to] put something in the books, hold those dates. It's a big chunk of time. It's four, five, six weeks of the court calendar; that's hard to fit in at the last minute," she said. "I would anticipate they block off the time while they go through all these motions and the DA's office figures out what it wants to do."

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy will reappear in court - but will her case be retried?

title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?
description: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midt
body: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.But are the polls accurate?Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate."Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate. It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeatPolling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.Figure caption, Voter voices: What issues matter most to Americans?There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science."I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?

title: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime
description: Warning: Distressing content and strong languageSamira says she never used to be political."I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BB
body: Warning: Distressing content and strong languageSamira says she never used to be political."I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BBC Panorama.But that all changed the day her only child was shot dead in front of her by Iranian security forces. Sixteen-year-old Sevda was taking part in protests against Iran's repressive regime that engulfed the country earlier this year - before the US and Israel launched widespread air strikes which killed the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.Samira's grief became fury as Iran's authorities then hindered, rather than helped, her search for her daughter's body, she says."I realised that finding Sevda wasn't the end, but just the beginning of all the harassment they put me through."Samira made a dramatic escape from Iran on foot, navigating dangerous mountainous terrain.She now lives abroad in hiding, describing herself as a "one-woman army fighting the regime". In a search for accountability and justice after her daughter's death, she is intent on naming the members of the security forces and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the protests."They'll bring me to the brink of death before they kill me, but finding me won't be easy… Return to normal life? There is no going back," she says.Samira is among several Iranians the BBC has spoken to since the start of the year. Some, still inside the country, told Panorama they wanted to speak out despite the risks, saying they had found it difficult to hold on to hope once the mass protests had been brutally crushed.The Iranian embassy in London told Panorama that peaceful and legitimate protests had been hijacked by foreign powers, including the US, which promoted violence, provided weapons and equipment, and compromised public security.Sevda was killed on 9 January as she and Samira took part in huge demonstrations on the outskirts of the capital Tehran which had begun the previous month. They had been sparked by economic discontent, before escalating into calls for an end to the country's Islamic Republic.Though Samira denies she was especially political then, she says her daughter was. Sevda's idols were two other young women - Mahsa Amini, whose death in custody after an alleged violation against the mandatory headscarf triggered mass protests, and Nika Shakarami, who was killed during a subsequent uprising against Iran's strict Islamic dress code for women."She kept them alive in her thoughts and always wanted to continue their path [of resistance]," Samira says.The day before Sevda was killed, the numbers protesting had been particularly high. Samira says she and Sevda had responded to a call by Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah (king), for demonstrations. "The security forces had lost control," she says.The swell in numbers had spooked Iran's government, and the following day a shoot-to-kill order was announced, Samira says. But she had thought it just an empty threat."They lied so much in Iran… We couldn't imagine a massacre of that scale."And they were reassured, she says, by US President Trump's promise that he had their backs.He had told US media on 8 January: "I have let [the Iranian authorities] know that if they start killing people, which they tend to do during their riots… we're going to hit them very hard."But nevertheless the crowds appeared smaller on the 9th, Samira says. Sevda seemed to know the risks, she says. Her daughter took off her earrings and gave them to her grandmother. She also shared her phone passcode with Samira.The mother and daughter gathered with the rest of the protesters. Sevda then stood on a dustbin and began leading a chant."It seemed there were more forces than people," Samira says of the area where they were. "I don't know how, within one day, they gathered so many… Basijis and IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] forces."The IRGC defends the country's Islamic establishment, and the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force are volunteers for the IRGC."A sniper fired from the roof of a building on our right. The bullet must have come from the rooftop. The bullet went through her heart. I couldn't even scream. I just stared at Sevda - her body lying lifeless. Blood was gushing out her mouth and nose. I couldn't believe it, I couldn't believe she was dying. Her eyes were still looking at me."Samira says she managed to get Sevda to hospital and she was told they were operating on her, but then the door opened and she saw Sevda had been zipped into a body bag.Sevda's body was taken away. Samira says it took her days to find her daughter again. Like many others, she found herself at one of Tehran's largest morgues."Teenagers - young boys and girls. So many had been killed," she cries."I died with every bag I unzipped. I'd never seen so many bodies. But I wouldn't give up."She finally found her daughter. "Three bodies were piled on top of Sevda. That's how we found her."Iranian authorities acknowledge that more than 3,000 people were killed in the protests, but claim some were members of the security forces. One human rights group, Hrana, however, estimates the number of dead stands at more than 7,000, most of them protesters. Finding Sevda's body was just the beginning of Samira's battle with the authorities, she says.To be allowed to take away the body for burial, she says she was forced to say that "terrorists" rather than the security forces had been responsible for Sevda's death."They did this to cover up what they'd done on 8 and 9 January, to hide how many people they had killed. They silenced families by telling them to say their loved ones were killed by Israeli or American terrorists."Nevertheless she was barred from visiting the grave after the funeral, or organising a tombstone, she says.And Samira says the harassment continued. A few days before the ceremony to mark 40 days since Sevda died - highly significant in Iranian culture - she says she was summoned by a local branch of the Ministry of Intelligence."They told me: 'You should give us an interview and say that Sevda was a Basiji and she was killed by the protesters. Then we will announce her [as] a martyr - you will then receive perks, a house, or anything that you want.'"She is sure this offer was prompted by fear, because she had shared Sevda's death with an Iranian media organisation based in London, once the internet had been reconnected in the country."It scared them that I was in touch with external networks or those outside Iran."To avoid giving the interview, Samira fled Iran as soon as the 40th day anniversary was over."I didn't want to trade with my child's blood."She says people smugglers helped her to escape. She crossed rivers and mountains to get to safety.A video she made of herself fleeing makes clear her fury."This crap government, these bastards, they've harassed me so much," she tells the camera as she marches along a mountain path bordered by a deep ravine.Samira says after she continued to give interviews to foreign media from abroad, she was charged in absentia with a string of offences, including "moharebeh" - waging war against God - which can carry the death penalty.To mark what would have been Sevda's 17th birthday, her relatives and friends held a vigil - with Samira watching from exile on a livestream."Then suddenly, the feed cut out," she says.She discovered that the event had been raided, she says, and some of her family and friends arrested by the IRGC.She says her family was warned by the authorities that, if they continued to gather at Sevda's grave, her body would be exhumed and moved elsewhere.Now, Samira shares the names, online, of Iranian security force members and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the 8 and 9 January protests she and Sevda joined."I want justice to be served for every single person whose name I expose, because they have killed so many young people. My goal is for them to be identified so they can be put on trial," she says.When one of the men Samira named online was later found dead, a regime supporter offered a $5,000 (£3,732) reward for information about her whereabouts, presuming she was responsible. Iranian state media has since reported the arrest of nine people in connection with the death.Despite the risks, Samira says she refuses to be silenced."Every day and every second without Sevda is very difficult for me. It's like a mother who has lost her heart, who has lost her being, has lost her life…"But the fact that Sevda is not breathing has made it possible for me to stand on my feet… to think about honouring her life and her path... all those bodies I saw, all those body bags I opened looking for Sevda, they all made me fight the Islamic Republic until my last breath."

schema.headline: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime

title: New Buy Now Pay Later rules - don't get caught out
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentIf you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have bee
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentIf you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have been tested to see if you can afford it.BNPL has always been a type of loan, usually paid back in instalments, but it's only been officially regulated since July.This means stricter background checks on your ability to repay. If you fail, then your purchase via BNPL will be blocked. If there's a chance of this happening to you, here are some ways to approach the situation.What are the new rules?BNPL lenders - such as Klarna, Clearpay and others - must now have regulator approval to operate, giving shoppers more access to refunds and independent rulings on complaints if things go wrong.But new affordability checks on each BNPL transaction could also leave you blocked from services for the first time.There are different affordability checks for different purchases, partially based on how much is borrowed.But, with the expensive festive season approaching, here's how to avoid being blocked when time and finances are tight. How do I avoid being blocked?Here are four things to consider if you find your account is closed or your borrowing limit has been massively reduced, from Sara Williams, a former volunteer debt adviser at Citizens Advice who posts tips as Debt Camel on social media.Slow down your purchases: is what you are buying essential or can you postpone it?Be more careful about what you buy to avoid needing a high credit limit to, for example, buy lots of clothes in different sizesCancel subscriptions to escape the trap of having to use BNPL to make up for the cost of previous paymentsTalk to debt charities for help and access to food bank vouchers if you are using BNPL for essentialsAvoid getting into debtIf you are struggling to make repayments on any type of loan - BNPL or otherwise - you should seek help before things spiral out of control.The government-backed, independent, MoneyHelper website, external has a guide to finding free debt advice near you, external.It also suggests writing down exactly what you owe, to help plan how you will repay the money.There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and a bill prioritiser, external to show which payments to make first and what to do if you miss a payment.You should also be sceptical of supposed debt solutions you might see on your social feeds.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues in this story? Share your experienceGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: New Buy Now Pay Later rules - don't get caught out

title: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
description: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade during the final leg
body: King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech that will touch on the issue.Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier wrote in the Guardian, external that he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and that the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".Browne went on to say that his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM). Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said."You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to the government's position.The Caribbean tour has again thrust the King into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed. Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology were a matter for government, not the Palace."His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to bat for Britain, the Realms and wider Commonwealth."In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", and said Britain "must face up to the past".His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by the King, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth. Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba, Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity"."True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".Later on Sunday, the King was left drenched and without an umbrella when a torrential downpour interrupted an Independence Day ceremony. The Queen was swiftly given an umbrella when the rain started, while the King was seen gesturing to be given one of his own.

schema.headline: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology

title: Parents' concerns to trigger urgent checks in A&E
description: A similar "early warning" system to identify acutely ill adults, including those with sepsis, is already in use in emergency and general NHS hospital
body: A similar "early warning" system to identify acutely ill adults, including those with sepsis, is already in use in emergency and general NHS hospital wards.More than 90 hospitals across England have been using the alert system in children's wards, with different age-appropriate assessments available for babies through to teenagers.The NHS has already said it will expand Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England. The rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review if they are worried that a patient's condition is getting worse and their concerns are not being responded to.The initiative is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis, in hospital following a bike accident. A coroner ruled that her family's concerns about her worsening condition were not listened to and she would probably have survived had she been moved to intensive care earlier. Martha's parents Merope and Paul came up with the idea of the rule in a bid to change the culture that contributed to her death.A&E units will have a dedicated phone number that can be called to trigger an urgent review of a patient's care.Duncan Burton, chief nursing officer for England, said the new early warning system for children in emergency departments was an "important next step in improving care for children and young people across England for this winter - and beyond".He added: "In fast-paced emergency departments, staff need to spot quickly when a child's condition is deteriorating."This standardised approach will help them recognise the warning signs, communicate concerns, and make timely decisions when every moment matters."The early warning system for children, PEWS, is a collaboration between NHS England and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and the Royal College of Nursing.

schema.headline: Parents' concerns to trigger urgent checks in A&E

title: Robotic surgery: 'All-island first' could cut gynae waiting lists
description: Like thousands of women in Northern Ireland, Colleen Crothers waited decades for medical help to treat chronic endometriosis - and, now thanks to an a
body: Like thousands of women in Northern Ireland, Colleen Crothers waited decades for medical help to treat chronic endometriosis - and, now thanks to an all-island first, she's hoping her long road will be a thing of the past."Robotic surgery came too late for me," she said. "I hope other women won't have to wait as long."She is talking about a new breakthrough for female patients in Northern Ireland - the Da Vinci gynae robot at Belfast City Hospital.Operated by humans, the robot's wrists can twist and turn in tight pelvic spaces and it is said to be more precise at complex surgery than a human hand because it is steadier.Belfast's Da Vinci robot is the first of its kind on the island of Ireland and one of only a few across the UK.It has the potential to massively reduce complex gynaecological surgical waiting lists in Northern Ireland, which affect thousands of women's physical and mental health and their ability to have children.With an average wait of about seven years for complex surgery, which involves several specialities, delayed treatment means some women require a hysterectomy, like Colleen at 41.She has lived with chronic endometriosis all of her adult life, having first begun to experience chronic period pain aged 14.But it took another 22 years before she was referred to gynaecology and a scan confirmed she had both adenomyosis and endometriosis."I missed out so much of family life due to daily pain - pain that went on for years," she said."I can't have children - I have had to have a hysterectomy and I'm in early menopause."To be told you can't have children is hard to swallow," she said.An urgent case, Colleen missed out on a Da Vinci operation by just weeks earlier this year.Da Vinci became part of the Belfast City Hospital's gynaecology team in May. It cost £2.4m and was funded through charitable donations for gynaecological services within the trust.To date it has performed 130 surgeries - 105 of them being on women with complex endometriosis - and four consultants have been trained to use the robot.It means that complex gynaecology cases are being treated as a priority and are not being bumped when other surgical cases, including cancer cases, come in.BBC News NI was given access to see the Da Vinci in action - and, like a real-life sci-fi creation, it has multiple towering robotic arms that hover over the patient.While humans are also in the theatre, it gives the surgeon a digital boost with incisions more precise and less invasive.Dr Hans Nagar, a consultant gynaecological surgeon and oncologist, is one of the surgeons trained to operate Da Vinci. He said women with complex endometriosis had previously been ill-served in Northern Ireland."They require complex surgery involving different specialists and now Da Vinci lets us do that," he said.

schema.headline: Robotic surgery: 'All-island first' could cut gynae waiting lists

title: Bonnie Tyler Christmas single Love, Light and Peace to be released
description: Bonnie Tyler Christmas single to be released as husband says he misses her every dayImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bonnie Tyler died aged 75
body: Bonnie Tyler Christmas single to be released as husband says he misses her every dayImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bonnie Tyler died aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this yearByRowenna HoskinBBC WalesBonnie Tyler's husband said it has "been a heartbreaking year" following her death and that he misses her "every single day".Tyler, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's last studio recording, Love, Light and Peace, will be released as a Christmas single on 13 November 2026.Tyler's husband of 50 years, Robert Sullivan, said: "Gaynor never stopped working. She loved singing, she loved her fans, and she poured her whole heart into these songs."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tyler's husband Robert Sullivan says it has been a "heart-breaking year"Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years.In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for Tyler at Swansea Minster."The only time she ever had off was during Covid, and even then she was still on Zoom doing interviews all the time," said Sullivan. "Between live shows she would stop by David Mackay's studio to work on all these new songs. "I know she would want people to hear them, and I am so proud of everything she left behind." After her last record contract expired, Tyler began self-releasing songs, with Yes I Can released on New Year's Day 2025, and then Only Love in March 2026, shortly before she became unwell. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bonnie had "no big ideas" about recording until she was spotted by a talent scoutLove, Light and Peace was written by Chrissie Hammond and 2026 Songwriters Hall of Fame inductee Terry Britten. It was produced by Britten and David Mackay, who both worked with Tyler at the start of her career. Tyler first worked with Britten in 1977, when he played guitar on her debut album, The World Starts Tonight. Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer of the last song she recorded.November would have seen Tyler in the middle of her Jubilee Tour across Europe, celebrating 50 years since her song Lost in France broke her into the UK Singles Chart in 1976.

schema.headline: Bonnie Tyler Christmas single Love, Light and Peace to be released

title: Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist
description: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is belie
body: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back."We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme."The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.

schema.headline: Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist

title: Australia omit Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc for England white-ball series
description: Australia's star pace trio of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc will not feature in the upcoming white-ball series against England.The ve
body: Australia's star pace trio of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc will not feature in the upcoming white-ball series against England.The veteran seamers played all three Tests in the recent 2-1 series defeat by South Africa and have been rested for the three-match ODI series that starts in Perth on 13 November.Cummins and Hazlewood have also been left out for the five-match T20 series that begins on 21 November, while Starc, 36, has already retired from the format.Fast bowler Mahli Beardman, 21, has been named in both squads and could make his international debut in ODIs, while uncapped wicketkeepers Sam Harper and Lachlan Shaw have been included for the T20s.Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Travis Head, Josh Inglis and Matt Renshaw, who also played in the South Africa series, are included for the ODIs but do not feature in the T20 squad.Although Cummins, 33, formally remains the ODI captain, he has only played one 50-over fixture since November 2024 and Mitchell Marsh, his frequent deputy and T20 skipper, will step in again for the longer format.Seamer Nathan Ellis, a white-ball regular, is only included in the T20 squad after suffering a side strain in the September ODI tour of South Africa and Zimbabwe, while fellow pacer Jack Edwards is named in both squads after making his debut on that trip.All-rounder Liam Scott, who played one 50-over match against Bangladesh in June, is recalled to the ODI squad, while spinners Nikhil Chaudhary and Joel Davies, who both made their only international T20 appearances on the same tour, are selected for the 20-over fixtures.Top-order batters Jake Fraser-McGurk and Mitchell Owen are recalled to the T20 squads after not featuring in recent series, while middle-order finisher Tim David is only selected for the shorter format despite recently returning to 50-over domestic cricket after an absence of four years.ODI and T20 squads: Mitchell Marsh (capt), Xavier Bartlett, Mahli Beardman, Jack Edwards, Spencer Johnson, Adam ZampaODI squad only: Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Ollie Peake, Matt Renshaw, Liam ScottT20 squad only: Nikhil Chaudhary, Tim David, Joel Davies, Nathan Ellis, Jake Fraser-McGurk, Sam Harper, Mitchell Owen, Lachlan ShawFollowing the final England T20 on 2 December, Australia will start a heavy pre-Ashes Test schedule in which Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood, 35, will be expected to feature frequently.They begin a four-match home Test series against New Zealand on 9 December before travelling for a five-Test series against India that starts on 21 January.They then face England in a one-off Test at the Melbourne Cricket Ground from 11 March, celebrating 150 years of Test cricket, prior to the Indian Premier League.Australia could also conceivably reach the World Test Championship final at the Oval on 9 June, shortly before the five-game Ashes series that runs from 18 June to 2 August.The ODI World Cup in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe will then begin on 7 October, with their veteran pace trio light on matches since they all featured in the 2023 final win in November 2023.Cummins has played in three ODIs since that match, while Hazlewood and Cummins have respectively featured in 14 and 11 of Australia's 35 games in that period.They have played just one game together since the World Cup, against Pakistan in Adelaide in November 2024, and all three missed the Champions Trophy in February last year.Ellis has played in 23 of Australia's 50-over games since the World Cup, while fellow seamers Xavier Bartlett, Spencer Johnson, who feature in both squads to face England, have played in 12 and seven ODIs in their careers.Joining them are 26-year-old Edwards, who played two ODIs against South Africa, and Beardman, who was first called-up into an Australia squad for a white-ball tour of England in 2024.Both Edwards and Beardman have appeared in a single T20, against Pakistan in Lahore in January, and the latter was a member of Australia's highly-rated 2024 under-19 World Cup winning squad.

schema.headline: Australia omit Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc for England white-ball series
